angles.label: Speed destroys evidence
angles.text: The first 48-72 hours are critical: after that, assets move through bridges, get layered in DEXs, or hit an exchange where KYC data exists but becomes harder to compel without immediate legal process. Many litigation teams delay forensic engagement until discovery is already open—by then the trail is cold.

angles.label: Tracing ≠ recovery
angles.text: A complete forensic chain-of-custody showing exactly where assets went is not the same as getting them back. You need that evidence for court, but recovery also depends on exchange cooperation, jurisdictional reach, and whether the destination is regulated. Knowing the difference shapes realistic timelines.

angles.label: Centralised exchange choke-point
angles.text: If stolen or disputed crypto reached a major regulated exchange, that's where leverage exists—but only if you move fast enough and have forensic evidence a court will accept. After that, the case becomes regulatory and procedural, not technical.

angles.label: Blockchain is a paper trail
angles.text: Unlike bank accounts, crypto holdings leave permanent on-chain records. If someone moved assets in the years before divorce proceedings, those transactions can be traced through exchanges or self-custody wallets—provided you know what to look for and have forensic expertise to present it properly.

angles.label: Self-custody hides nothing long
angles.text: A private wallet holds assets but doesn't hide the movement. If crypto was purchased, sold, or moved to an exchange at any point, there's a forensic record linked to identity, timing, and value. The technical difficulty is for the spouse claiming there's nothing; the advantage is for the one seeking evidence.

angles.label: Valuation date matters legally
angles.text: Courts need a snapshot of what was owned on the cutoff date (separation, filing, valuation date) and its worth that day. Forensic evidence must show not just existence but timing and value at that specific moment—mixing that up with current holdings is a common mistake that weakens cases.

angles.label: AML teams need clean transaction trails
angles.text: Source-of-funds verification is not about price history; it's about proving the KYC on-ramp was legitimate and that the money arriving at an exchange is traceable to a genuine economic activity or prior holding. A clean chain from bank to exchange to wallet is what regulators and exchanges actually want to see.

angles.label: Layering is the tell
angles.text: When funds hit an exchange and immediately move through multiple swaps, bridges, or DEXs before returning—that's a pattern that raises flags. Legitimate source-of-funds verification looks for direct, documented paths; complexity without explanation is what triggers deeper scrutiny.

angles.label: Timing and identity alignment
angles.text: Source-of-funds checks fail when there's a gap between who owns the wallet and who sent the originating funds, or when timing doesn't match the stated economic activity. Forensic evidence that closes these gaps—KYC data, bank statements, transaction logs—is what actually satisfies compliance teams.

angles.label: VASP rules remake customer identity
angles.text: MiCA's customer information requirements for crypto transfers are stricter than many firms realise: you need to know not just your customer but the beneficiary on the other side. That means exchanges and custodians need forensic-grade visibility into who is moving what, and where it goes.

angles.label: Stablecoin issuers face traceability burden
angles.text: MiCA treats stablecoins as payment instruments with capital and transparency rules. Issuers now need to demonstrate they can trace redemptions and identify bad actors using their coins—that's a forensic and AML problem, not just a product problem.

angles.label: Supervision analytics expose the gaps
angles.text: MiCA compliance supervisors are looking at transaction patterns and counterparty risk across Europe. Firms that can't produce clean forensic evidence of their own customer flows and sanctions screening will show up in supervision analytics as high-risk. Being audit-ready before the supervisor asks is now table-stakes.

angles.label: Wallet clustering is not enough
angles.text: AML teams often group addresses by shared ownership (clustering) but stop there. Real AML work requires understanding the economic logic: why did this cluster move funds to that exchange, and can you confirm from KYC data that the two sides are the same entity? Data alone doesn't answer compliance questions.

angles.label: Sanctions screening must be on-chain aware
angles.text: Screening custodian lists against wallet addresses is a common practice, but it's incomplete. Bad actors use mixers, bridges, and layering. AML teams that rely only on direct-match screening will miss funds flowing from or to sanctioned parties through intermediate hops—forensic tracing catches what screening alone misses.

angles.label: Timing of red flags matters
angles.text: A transaction that looks suspicious at T+2 hours might look completely normal at T+30 days once you trace the originating source or destination. AML teams need forensic evidence available in near-real-time to make hold or escalation decisions, not post-hoc explanations after funds have moved too far.

angles.label: Forensics must align with legal process
angles.text: Under NIS2 and DORA, you're reporting to authorities anyway; your forensic evidence will eventually be scrutinised by prosecutors or regulators. Evidence collected in a way that's admissible and chain-of-custody clean from day one saves months of friction later—and makes law enforcement's job possible.

angles.label: Timing: ransom demand to payment window
angles.text: Ransom payments create a permanent blockchain record, but only if they happen. The period between the demand and any payment is when freeze requests, asset recovery orders, or law enforcement action can actually make a difference. After the payment moves through an exchange or mixer, options shrink rapidly.

angles.label: Dual mandate: pay now, trace later
angles.text: Organisations often make ransom payments under duress without forensic support, then ask for recovery afterward. A parallel forensic engagement during the incident gives negotiators real data on whether the group is real and previously reliable, and positions you for either recovery or prosecution evidence if the payment goes to an exchange.

angles.label: Forensic evidence is supervisory evidence
angles.text: NIS2 incident reporting to authorities isn't a checkbox; it's a formal record that will be reviewed by regulators and potentially law enforcement. Evidence collected under proper forensic standards—chain of custody, contemporaneous documentation, expert analysis—is what actually satisfies the obligation rather than a narrative summary.

angles.label: 24-hour reporting clock starts at discovery
angles.text: NIS2 requires notification within 24 hours of discovering a significant incident; the clock doesn't restart when you've fully investigated. Many organisations delay reporting to get 'complete' forensic findings, then realise they've missed the window. Early reporting with preliminary forensic findings and a detailed followup is legally sound and operationally better.

angles.label: Crypto incidents are NIS2 incidents
angles.text: Ransomware payments, wallet compromises, or funds theft involving crypto are operational incidents under NIS2 scope if the organisation is in-scope. They trigger the same reporting obligations as traditional cyber incidents—and the forensic standard is the same: what can be demonstrated to the regulator with evidence.

angles.label: Third-party crypto services are DORA dependencies
angles.text: DORA requires mapping and testing of critical third-party dependencies, including custodians, settlement layers, and wallets. If your operational resilience depends on a blockchain bridge or a crypto custodian, you need to document the failure modes and have forensic visibility into how funds actually move through that dependency.

angles.label: Incident classification starts with forensics
angles.text: DORA incident reporting thresholds depend partly on impact—was it a 15-minute outage or a total breach? In crypto operations, forensic evidence of what actually happened (which addresses, which assets, which timespan) is what determines whether an incident meets DORA thresholds and what you must report.

angles.label: Testing crypto infrastructure under DORA
angles.text: DORA's resilience testing requirements apply to crypto settlement and custody arrangements too. If you're testing a bridge or a decentralised exchange integration, you need forensic-grade visibility into transaction outcomes and timing under failure scenarios—which is a forensic investigation problem, not just an operational test.

angles.label: On-chain data is not the investigation
angles.text: A blockchain record shows what moved and when, but it doesn't explain why, who authorised it, or whether it was theft or legitimate transaction. Investigation means connecting on-chain evidence to off-chain facts: KYC data, email logs, device records, bank transfers. Forensics without investigation is just data archaeology.

angles.label: Mixer and bridge opacity is not absolute
angles.text: Funds passing through tumblers or bridges don't disappear; they emerge somewhere, usually an exchange. The forensic job is tracing the likely path based on transaction size, timing, and token type, then confirming identity when the assets hit regulated infrastructure. Mixers delay but don't erase the trail.

angles.label: Exchange cooperation is the leverage point
angles.text: A complete forensic trace pointing to a major exchange means you can compel cooperation through law enforcement, civil process, or regulatory request. But only if the evidence is court-ready and the exchange is regulated and responsive. Forensic investigations that end in an unregulated DEX or peer-to-peer transfer have no enforcement lever.

angles.label: Evidence standard: court-ready, not just technical
angles.text: Law enforcement needs forensic evidence that will survive cross-examination and chain-of-custody scrutiny in court, not just a technical explanation of how fraud happened. Many private investigators hand over raw blockchain analysis that doesn't meet evidentiary standards; prosecutors can't use it without forensic re-work and expert testimony.

angles.label: Speed of evidence preservation matters
angles.text: If a suspect has not yet moved funds to an exchange, law enforcement can sometimes issue a preservation order freezing them on-chain—but only in the hours before the assets are transferred. After that, the path becomes regulatory (exchange cooperation) or international (treaties, mutual legal assistance). Forensic evidence is most valuable while law enforcement still has technical options.

angles.label: Ransomware demands create cooperation opportunities
angles.text: In ransomware cases, the ransom demand, negotiation logs, and payment timeline are evidence that law enforcement can use to identify the group and link demands to actual payments. Parallel forensic investigation during negotiation—confirming the group, tracing the address, preparing for law enforcement handoff—multiplies the prosecution value of the eventual payment.

angles.label: Blockchain je trajni zapis
angles.text: Za razliko od klasičnih prevar, kriptovalutne prevare ostavljaju večni otisak na lancu blokova. Ako je neko ukrao sredstva ili prevarom nagovorio nekoga da pošalje novac, taj transfer se nikada ne može obrisati niti promijeniti—to postaje forenzički dokaz koji se može koristiti u istražnim i sudskim procedurama.

angles.label: Od izmjene do razmjene
angles.text: Većina kriptovalutnih prevara završi na reguliranoj burzi: tamo se mogu prisiliti prema zakonu ili nadzoru da otvore podatke o korisniku. Forenzička analiza koja pokazuje točnu putanju od žrtve do burze čini slučaj rješivim; analiza koja završi u nereguliranoj DEX ili peer-to-peer transakciji nema poluge za povratak.

angles.label: Brzina je kritična
angles.text: Prva 48 sati nakon što su sredstva dosegla burzu su kada je dostupna najveća poluga: tehnička analiza, zahtjevi za podatke, privremene mjere. Kasnije se slučaj pretvara u regulatorna pitanja i međunarodne procedure.早 forenzička uključenost može biti razlika između mogućnosti povrata i samo dokumentacije.

posts.title: Orange Cyberdefense’s Security Navigator 2026 shows that even though law enforcement actions against cybercrime increased from 2021 to 2025, the number of cybercrime attackers and
posts.author: Orange Cyberdefense
posts.snippet:
Orange Cyberdefense’s Security Navigator 2026 shows that even though law enforcement actions against cybercrime increased from 2021 to 2025, the number of cybercrime attackers and incidents didn’t shrink in response. They multiplied.
 
The report provides a systematically constructed database of all the publicly announced law enforcement actions against different kinds of cybercrime from 2021 to mid-2025. The numbers look encouraging at first:
 
418: the number of law enforcement actions, including arrests, takedowns, charges, sentences, sanctions, seizures in that period.
 
59: documented cases of arrest against cyber-extortion in that time – making cyber-extortion the form of cybercrime most likely to lead to arrest.
 
But when you see these against the staggering statistics of how cybercrime has scaled faster than the law enforcement actions intended to counter it, the picture reveals a dark truth.
 
89: The number of active extortion groups operating during this period – this number has tripled since 2020, where there were around 33 extortion groups globally.
 
53: The number of victims per cybercrime actor or attacker – this is up from 43 in the previous period.
 
And, despite the fact that two of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) cybercrime syndicates, Black Basta and Lockbit, have both been disrupted, the number of other syndicates’ victims in Europe increased dramatically:
 
324%: The rise in the number of victims of Russian-speaking RaaS cybercrime organisation Qilin, which has been in operation since 2022.
 
168%: The rise in the number of victims of Akila, another financially motivated RaaS gang, active since 2023.
 
These figures show that as soon as one cybercrime syndicate is taken down, there is a space created for a new one, or several more, to fill it.
 
The findings of the Security Navigator 2026 don’t tell the story of law enforcement failing – because it isn’t. The findings show the rapid emergence of Crime as a Service, leading to cybercrime becoming industrialised, and cybercrime becoming easier and cheaper to commit as time goes by.
 
Download the Security Navigator 2026 here to get a fuller picture of the modern global threat landscape: https://ow.ly/kfbS50Z6zy4
posts.reason: Law enforcement effectiveness data on ransomware and extortion groups directly interests CISOs, risk officers, and law enforcement; discussion-worthy analysis that Bloctopus could credibly expand on.

comments.text: The 53-victims-per-actor figure is the number that matters most from a forensics standpoint: it means the marginal cost of a new victim is near zero once infrastructure and affiliates are in place, so arrests alone can't outpace onboarding into RaaS programmes.

Does the report break down how many of the 418 actions actually led to asset seizure versus just arrest or sanction? Attribution and prosecution are one thing, recovering the extorted funds is a very different success rate.

We see the same pattern from the tracing side: taking down one operator's infrastructure rarely touches the affiliate network or the money-laundering layer downstream, which is usually still running the next day under a different brand.

Maritime Cybersecurity Wake-Up Call 
The shipping and logistics sector is facing an unprecedented wave of sophisticated cyber threats. Over the last month alone, three major incidents have redefined the digital risk landscape for global maritime operations:

1. The Adriatic Port Authority Ransomware Crisis

Cause: A highly targeted, sophisticated cyberattack by the Anubis ransomware group.
Effect: Complete exfiltration of highly sensitive emergency plans, employee records, and internal communications, resulting in severe regional logistics disruptions and a $10 million ransom demand.
Solutions: Organizations must deploy advanced behavioral endpoint detection and response (EDR) alongside zero-trust network segmentation (Technical). Equally vital is establishing robust, offline backup governance and immutable data recovery workflows to completely neutralize financial extortion leverage (Non-Technical).

2. APT28’s Rapid Transport & Logistics Espionage

Cause: Russian-linked state-sponsored group APT28 (Fancy Bear) rapidly weaponized a newly disclosed Microsoft security bypass flaw.
Effect: Instant deployment of "BEARDSHELL" backdoors and email-stealing malware, compromising maritime transport agencies across Europe and the UAE within 24 hours of patch release.
Solutions: Implement automated, high-priority patch management systems and continuous threat-hunting feeds to catch zero-day exploits (Technical). Organizations must shift toward strict vendor risk management frameworks and rapid incident-response communication drills to counter state-sponsored agility (Non-Technical).

3. USCG Cyber Command CTIME Intelligence Warning

Cause: The accelerated adoption of AI, dangerous IT-OT convergence, and reliance on unpatched legacy operational systems.
Effect: Critical vulnerabilities across the marine environment, with the USCG noting that even modern AI-driven defense platforms are failing due to weak configurations.
Solutions: Enforce strict Operational Technology (OT) firewalls, legacy device shielding, and rigorous configuration management audits for all AI tools (Technical). Senior leadership must mandate standardized maritime cyber-hygiene training and comprehensive IT-OT alignment strategies across entire fleets (Non-Technical).

The Bottom Line:
The ultimate truth linking these threats is that the maritime industry cannot out-innovate adversaries with tools alone if underlying systemic vulnerabilities are ignored. The industry frequently overlooks two critical, fundamental pillars: ruthless configuration integrity and human-centric security culture. We invest millions in cutting-edge AI defenses, yet allow them to fail due to basic misconfigurations. True resilience requires matching advanced technical safeguards with an unyielding corporate culture of transparency, continuous testing, and proactive cyber hygiene from the boardroom to the cargo deck.
#MaritimeSecurity #CyberSecurity #Ransomware #SupplyChain #Logistics #OTSecurity #USCG
posts.reason: Maritime ransomware and incident response are relevant to NIS2/DORA scope, but the post reads more like vendor solutions marketing than open discussion.

comments.text: On the Adriatic Port case, the detail worth stressing is that immutable backups neutralise the encryption threat but do nothing against the exfiltration/extortion threat - those need separate legal and negotiation playbooks, not just recovery tooling.

For the APT28 case, was the 24-hour window from patch release to exploitation measured against the vendor's disclosure timeline or against when the PoC went public? That gap tells you whether patch management or detection is the real bottleneck.

In ransomware response work, the IT-OT convergence point you raise on USCG is usually where crisis coordination breaks down fastest - technical containment and legal/regulatory notification clocks run on different timelines and nobody owns the handoff between them.

#AMustRead 🔆
🟡"Why digital asset fraud victims won't sue"by Edmund Yong

📌 #Summary
The article details why victims of cryptocurrency/digital asset fraud rarely pursue legal action to recover stolen funds. Through a scenario involving a buyer scammed during a cross-border Bitcoin purchase, the author highlights how the decentralized, cross-border, and anonymous nature of blockchains creates severe jurisdiction, identification, and legal enforcement hurdles that make civil litigation practically ineffective.

💡 #KeyTakeaways
 1. The Jurisdictional Nightmare ("Omni-territorial"):Unlike centralized cloud servers, public blockchains operate on global node networks. Determining #where the crime occurred or #whichcourt has jurisdiction is nearly impossible.

2. Anonymous / Non-Existent Defendants: Victims often face "Persons Unknown" or automated bots (dApps/DAOs) that are not recognized as legal entities that can be sued.

 3. High Obstacles to Legal Discovery:
 3.1 Tracing funds to a crypto exchange (DAX) is often not enough to freeze them quickly.
3.2 Courts rarely grant disclosure orders to compel exchanges to reveal customer names.
3.3 Serving court documents (e.g., via NFT to a wallet address) is tricky and unreliable.
3.4 Low Recovery Rates:
~78% of crypto crimes are never reported to authorities.
~93% of victims do not even report within 24 hours.

posts.title: Privacy coins and privacy layers create different compliance architectures
posts.author: Aleksandr Drachev
posts.snippet:
Privacy coins and privacy layers create different compliance architectures

In compliance discussions, privacy-enhancing technologies are often grouped into a single high-risk category.

From a regulatory perspective, that simplification is increasingly difficult to justify.

The real distinction is not between technologies that are "private" and those that are "transparent." It is between technologies that create fundamentally different models of compliance evidence.

Privacy coins such as Monero - or shielded transactions on Zcash - are designed to conceal transactional information at the protocol level. Depending on the implementation, investigators may have limited access to counterparties, transaction flows or transferred amounts using conventional blockchain analytics.

For compliance teams, this is not simply a visibility issue. It changes the availability of evidence used for transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, AML investigations and forensic analysis.

Privacy layers built on public blockchains present a different challenge.

Protocols such as Railgun or Aztec are designed to provide transactional confidentiality while operating within ecosystems that can support varying degrees of selective disclosure, cryptographic attestations or other protocol-specific mechanisms for demonstrating compliance when appropriate.

That distinction matters.

From a risk-based perspective, the key compliance question is no longer "Does this protocol provide privacy?"

It is "What evidence remains available to satisfy regulatory obligations, and under what conditions can that evidence be lawfully accessed or demonstrated?"

Those are fundamentally different risk models.

Treating every privacy-enhancing technology as presenting the same compliance exposure risks producing controls that are both overinclusive and operationally ineffective.

As regulated institutions expand their participation in digital assets, compliance will increasingly move beyond binary assumptions of transparency versus anonymity. Future control frameworks will be built around evidentiary access, auditability and proportional disclosure - not around the mere presence of privacy features.

Compliance has never been about maximizing visibility for its own sake.

Its objective is to ensure that institutions retain sufficient control, defensible evidence and effective risk management to meet their legal and regulatory obligations - even as the underlying technology continues to evolve.

For protocols like Railgun with selective disclosure, has any regulator actually specified what counts as 'sufficient' disclosure for AML purposes, or is that still being tested case by case?

posts.title: When crypto is stolen, the instinct is often to write it off. The funds are gone, the trail is cold, and recovery feels like a long shot.
posts.author: Pinnacle Blocks
posts.snippet:
When crypto is stolen, the instinct is often to write it off. The funds are gone, the trail is cold, and recovery feels like a long shot.

That assumption is usually wrong.

Every transaction on a public blockchain is permanently recorded. Unlike cash or a wire transfer, stolen crypto does not simply vanish. It moves, and every movement is visible to anyone who knows how to read it.

Criminals understand this. They use mixers, chain-hops and layered wallets to break the trail. But those techniques are not invisible. They produce their own patterns, and trained analysts can follow them.

The most important variable is time. The sooner a blockchain forensics investigation begins, the greater the chance of tracking funds before they reach a cooperative exchange or a jurisdiction where recovery becomes much harder. Delay compresses options.

Recovery is never guaranteed. But a digital asset investigation will almost always tell you more than you currently know, including whether recovery has a realistic path and what that path looks like.

If funds have been taken, the question worth asking is not whether a trace is possible. It is how quickly one can begin.

posts.title: All hail the UK’s Proceeds of Crime Act (#POCA) 2002.
posts.author: Ashley Fairbrother
posts.snippet:
All hail the UK’s Proceeds of Crime Act (#POCA) 2002.

I recently read The DOJ’s Deals with the Devils, (https://lnkd.in/eBgmqmEv) which raises a sad and uncomfortable question: who should come first in an asset recovery regime - the victim or the State?

Over the past two months I’ve been helping a victim who lost approximately US$6.5 million in a sophisticated phishing fraud.

The proceeds were rapidly laundered through multiple wallets and routed towards Tornado Cash and other mixers in the usual way. Despite that, within around 48 hours of the theft, working alongside what I genuinely believe are some of the world’s best crypto investigators at ZeroShadow, and in close and rapid collaboration with #UKLawEnforcement, US$2 million had successfully been traced, demixed and frozen.

This is precisely where the UK’s legislative framework shines. It is also why we have focused on and become known for working so effectively alongside UK law enforcement in fast-moving crypto investigations.

Thereafter, within a month we worked with the police to obtain seven separate Crypto Wallet Freezing Orders, converting voluntary freezes into court orders. The legislation is fast, relatively inexpensive and, crucially, designed to preserve assets so victims can seek recovery under s.303Z51 POCA.

The focus is to protect the victim’s property.

The article contrasts that with aspects of the US civil forfeiture regime, where, once assets are forfeited, victims may have to pursue a (discretionary) administrative remission process and do not necessarily have priority over the government’s interest in the proceeds. That clearly does not strikes the right balance IMO!

The comparison below, taken from the court filing, illustrates the difference rather neatly.

In Turkey, where ownership is readily identifiable, the law prioritises returning property directly to victims. The UK approach, particularly under the newer POCA crypto provisions, is philosophically much closer to that model than to the US forfeiture regime.

For all the criticism POCA often attracts, cases like this remind me how fortunate UK victims are to have access to these tools. It’s  also no coincidence that so many victims from around the world look to English lawyers and the English courts when trying to recover stolen digital assets.

Thanks to Nick Smart for sending this to me last night!

Well done Nivie Kaul ! 

#cryptofraud #fraud
Edmonds Marshall McMahon

posts.title: A compliance officer should be able to connect suspicious transaction behaviour to the possible predicate offence behind it.
posts.author: Abraham Udu, ACA, CCI, CAMS, CFCS, CSOE, CESGR, CRCMP, CISRCP
posts.snippet:
A compliance officer should be able to connect suspicious transaction behaviour to the possible predicate offence behind it.

This is where Transaction Monitoring moves from alert management to financial crime intelligence.

Once an investigation establishes reasonable grounds for suspicion, the analyst should ask:

What crime could have generated, facilitated, or benefited from these funds?

Under Nigeria's Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (MLPPA), predicate offences are not limited to one narrow category of crime. The framework captures a broad range of unlawful activities, consistent with FATF standards, while also allowing other criminal acts recognised under Nigerian law to fall within the predicate-offence framework.

For practical AFC risk assessment, professionals should be familiar with typologies involving:

🔹 Fraud and cybercrime

🔹 Corruption, bribery and abuse of office

🔹 Drug trafficking

🔹 Terrorism and terrorist financing

🔹 Kidnapping and ransom proceeds

🔹 Human trafficking and migrant smuggling

🔹 Armed robbery and organised crime

🔹 Smuggling and illicit trafficking

🔹 Tax crimes and tax evasion

🔹 Illegal mining and environmental crimes

🔹 Proliferation-related offences

🔹 Counterfeiting and forgery

🔹 Insider trading and market manipulation

🔹 Piracy and other serious criminal activities

The practical workflow should be:

Transaction/Activity → Red Flag → Typology → Possible Predicate Offence → Investigation → STR/Intelligence → NFIU Analysis → Law Enforcement Investigation

For example, unusual cash deposits followed by ransom payments may point towards kidnapping-for-ransom typologies. A network of accounts receiving unexplained inflows from public-sector contractors may indicate corruption or procurement fraud. Crypto transfers connected to ransomware wallets may indicate cybercrime proceeds.

This is why compliance professionals need more than AML regulation knowledge.

They must understand criminal typologies, transaction behaviour, local context, and the legal framework well enough to connect financial activity to the potential underlying crime.

The objective is not for the compliance officer to prosecute the crime.

It is to provide the NFIU and competent authorities with actionable financial intelligence that helps them identify the criminal enterprise, investigate the predicate offence, trace the proceeds, and ultimately pursue asset recovery.

The better we map predicate offences to financial behaviour, the more useful our AML intelligence becomes.

#AML #FinancialCrime #PredicateOffences #TransactionMonitoring #FinancialIntelligence #NFIU #Fraud #Cybercrime #Corruption #Kidnapping #HumanTrafficking #DrugTrafficking #Compliance #RiskManagement #AssetRecovery #Nigeria

Crypto Fraud Recovery: Recent criminal proceedings reported by the media, concerning an alleged cryptocurrency fraud, reveal a good example of how complex crypto fraud investigations are often most effective when the private and public sectors work together.

The case involves allegations of a sophisticated fraud targeting cryptocurrency holders and demonstrates the challenges law enforcement faces in investigating increasingly technical financial crime. Whilst the premise of the fraud is deceptively simple, it's highly sophisticated from a psychological perspective, extremely effective, and the technical infrastructure used to facilitate and launder the proceeds is anything but simple.

Before the police investigation commenced, the matter had initially been reported to Report Fraud but did not progress further.

Edmonds Marshall McMahon was instructed by the victim to investigate. 

Working alongside the outstanding team at iSanctuary, we traced assets on-chain to obtain Norwich Pharmacal and Bankers Trust Orders against cryptocurrency exchanges, before returning to the High Court to obtain similar relief against internet service providers. Those enquiries enabled us to identify individuals allegedly connected to the fraud and develop actionable intelligence.

That intelligence was provided to law enforcement, who were able to exercise the powers available to them. As has now been publicly reported (https://lnkd.in/eUVGaHWk), the subsequent investigation has resulted in arrests, asset seizures and ongoing criminal proceedings.

Cases such as this demonstrate that tackling sophisticated crypto-enabled fraud is rarely the responsibility of one organisation, or one sector, alone.

The private sector has specialist expertise, civil investigative tools and the ability to dedicate time and significant resources to developing intelligence. Law enforcement may not always have the resources, particularly in the early stages of an investigation, but it has the powers to investigate criminality, secure evidence and bring prosecutions.

When those capabilities are combined, victims stand a far greater chance of seeing justice and meaningful outcomes. It's a model that we fully embrace at Edmonds Marshall McMahon to help victims of these increasing crimes.

Thanks to iSanctuary for their excellent work on this investigation, to the Police officers who progressed the matter once it was referred, and to our dedicated team at EMM, Rhys Evans and Edis Balci.

A 12-week trial is set for Chelmsford Crown Court from 24 May next year,

For those interested in the case, a summary of the reported proceedings can be found here: https://lnkd.in/eaTFESPU

posts.title: An AI agent just ran a cyberattack on the finance ministry. Without a human in the loop.

An AI agent just ran a cyberattack on the finance ministry. Without a human in the loop.

This week, researchers uncovered an operation against Thailand's Ministry of Finance where the attacker deployed Hermes - an open-source AI agent - in what the tool's own documentation calls "YOLO mode." No human approval at any step. The agent did the reconnaissance, found privilege escalation paths, deployed web shells, and tested credentials against internal mail servers. 585 files recovered. Active compromise of government financial infrastructure.

I've seen automated attacks before. This is different.

The speed is different. The consistency is different. And critically - the tool is free, open-source, and anyone can download it today.

DORA came into force in January. The regulation was written with exactly this threat profile in mind: sophisticated, fast, hard to attribute, targeting financial infrastructure. The pillars are clear - ICT risk management, mandatory incident reporting, third-party tool risk, operational resilience testing.

What I'm seeing in most DORA compliance programs is the documentation is there. The policies are filed. The ICT risk register exists.

But the threat model inside that register still assumes a human behind the keyboard.

That assumption is now outdated.

If your SOC detection rules, your incident response playbooks, and your third-party risk assessments were all designed around human-speed attacks - you have a gap. AI agents operate differently. They don't take breaks. They don't make the same mistakes humans do. And they don't show up in your logs the way a person would.

DORA compliance isn't a one-time project. The threat it was designed to address just changed.

Has your ICT risk framework been updated since AI agents became operational weapons?

🔒 𝗣𝗖𝗜 𝗗𝗦𝗦 (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
→ Who it’s for: Any business that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data
→ Focus: Protecting payment card transactions and cardholder data specifically
→ Key points: Secure network architecture, encryption of cardholder data, access control, regular vulnerability scanning, and continuous monitoring/logging
→ Where it’s used: Retail, e-commerce, banking, and any merchant or payment processor globally
🌍 𝗜𝗦𝗢 𝟮𝟳𝟬𝟬𝟭
→ Who it’s for: Any organization wanting a formal, certifiable Information Security Management System (ISMS)
→ Focus: Broad, risk-based approach to managing information security across the whole business — not just one data type
→ Key points: Risk assessment and treatment, defined security policies, asset management, continual improvement (PDCA cycle)
→ Where it’s used: Internationally recognized; common requirement in vendor/client due diligence across every industry
🛡️ 𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗧 (commonly referring to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework)
→ Who it’s for: Primarily US federal agencies and contractors, but adopted voluntarily worldwide
→ Focus: A flexible framework (not a certification) built around five functions — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
→ Key points: Risk management guidance rather than strict pass/fail controls; highly adaptable to organization size and maturity
→ Where it’s used: US government, critical infrastructure, and widely as a benchmark framework globally
🏦 𝗗𝗢𝗥𝗔 (Digital Operational Resilience Act)
→ Who it’s for: Financial entities and their critical ICT third-party providers operating in the EU
→ Focus: Operational resilience — ensuring the financial sector can withstand, respond to, and recover from ICT-related disruptions
→ Key points: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk oversight, information sharing
→ Where it’s used: Mandatory across the EU financial sector since January 2025
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲:
• PCI DSS = narrow scope (payment data), mandatory if you touch card data
• ISO 27001 = broad scope (all information assets), voluntary certification, globally recognized
• NIST = flexible guidance framework, not a certification, mostly US-driven but globally referenced
• DORA = EU regulation, sector-specific (finance), focused on operational resilience, not just data protection
Knowing which standard applies and why is often the difference between a compliance program that’s built to satisfy an auditor and one that’s actually built to reduce risk.

posts.title: 𝑰𝒔 𝑫𝑶𝑹𝑨 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒄𝒚𝒃𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒄𝒖𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒚?

That’s the question I found myself asking while reading about the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). At first, it looked like another regulation focused on cybersecurity. But the more I read, the more I felt that cybersecurity isn’t actually the main message. What if DORA isn’t trying to prevent every cyberattack? What if it’s trying to change the way organizations think about risk?

No system is perfect. Technology fails, people make mistakes, and new threats appear every day. If that’s the reality organizations operate in, then measuring success by whether “nothing went wrong” no longer seems realistic. The more I thought about it, the more I realized that perhaps we’ve been asking the wrong question.
Instead of asking how to eliminate every possible risk, maybe we should be asking something different: Can an organization continue to operate when something does go wrong?

To me, that’s where DORA becomes interesting. I don’t see it as another cybersecurity regulation. I see it as a framework that shifts the focus from prevention to resilience. Preventing incidents will always be important, but DORA seems to recognize something many organizations already know: prevention isn’t always enough. What matters just as much is how quickly an organization can respond, recover, and continue operating when an incident inevitably occurs.

That changes the conversation. Risk management is no longer only about reducing the likelihood of disruption. It’s also about reducing the consequences when disruption happens. In other words, the goal isn’t to create an organization where nothing ever goes wrong. It’s to create one where a single incident doesn’t become a business crisis.

Studying finance and risk management has made me appreciate this shift in perspective. We often evaluate risk management by looking at what was prevented, but perhaps we should also evaluate it by looking at how organizations perform when prevention fails.

This is simply my perspective based on what I’ve read so far. As always, I’d be happy to hear different opinions.

posts.title: I built a counterparty monitoring system for a crypto firm last month.
posts.author: Viktor Andriichuk
posts.snippet:
I built a counterparty monitoring system for a crypto firm last month.

The ESMA register is public. Downloading the CSV takes 30 seconds. Matching your counterparties against it takes considerably longer — because almost nobody uses their legal name.

You know them as "Bitfinex." The register says "iFinex Inc." Their EU entity files under a third name. Their custody subsidiary is a fourth.

One counterparty. Four names. Three jurisdictions. Zero overlap with what's in your system.

Multiply by 200 counterparties. Cross-reference against weekly register updates. Factor in subsidiaries, group structures, and transliterations across alphabets.

That's entity resolution — and it's the real engineering challenge behind counterparty monitoring. Not downloading a list. Proving that every entity in your transaction flow is still authorised, continuously, across names you didn't know existed.

A CSV is public. Entity resolution is the product.

How many names does your biggest counterparty operate under?

#MiCA #CASP #Engineering #Compliance #DigitalAssets

comments.text: The transliteration problem gets worse once you add on-chain entity resolution — the same custodial cluster can span dozens of deposit addresses across chains, and matching those to a single legal entity is a parallel version of the same problem you're describing off-chain.

posts.title: Someone sent me a link yesterday. Tokenization
posts.author: Martín Pérez
posts.snippet:
Someone sent me a link yesterday. Tokenization
infrastructure for banks and asset managers.
Compliance-first, chain-agnostic, ISO 27001.

The site is genuinely well built. Better than most
of what actually works.

Seven products. Tokenization platform, settlement
layer, identity passport, an islamic finance protocol,
decentralized compute and clean energy, and AI-assisted
DAO governance.

Seven. From one team.

The "request a demo" button opens your mail client
with someone's personal address in it.

And there's a token presale. $0.31, ten phases,
invite code.

Nobody selling infrastructure to a bank raises money
from strangers on the internet. They raise from the
bank. That's the whole point of selling to banks.

What annoys me is that the underlying thing is real.

I spend my week reading ERC-3643 implementations.
Compliance encoded in the token contract, transfers
that revert when the receiving wallet isn't on the
whitelist. It works. Money market funds, private credit,
short-term paper. MiCA is in force. This is happening.

It's also the least exciting thing in crypto.
It's custody agreements and transfer agents and
someone in operations explaining why the redemption
didn't settle. There's no presale. There's no thread.

So the attention goes somewhere else, and the actual
work ships in silence.

If you're a lawyer or an accountant, a client is going
to send you one of these links this year and ask what
you think. You won't be able to read the contracts.

But you can ask where the revenue comes from.
If the answer is the token itself, you're done.
That one question filters most of it.

I'm not saying this project is a fraud. I don't know.
I spent twenty minutes on it and stopped.

What I know is that I stopped at the presale, and I'd
stop again.

posts.title: The MiCA licensing race is over. Less than 20% of EU banks offer crypto services. Now compliance costs will sort the industry into buyers and sellers.
posts.author: Dionisijs Markovs
posts.snippet:
The MiCA licensing race is over. Less than 20% of EU banks offer crypto services. Now compliance costs will sort the industry into buyers and sellers.

According to CoinDesk, the next phase of MiCA is about whether firms can sustain the ongoing cost of operating under full regulation. The expectation from lawyers and industry leaders: a wave of mergers, acquisitions, and partnerships between crypto firms and traditional financial institutions.

Simon Schneider, CEO of Sygnum Europe, puts it directly: less than 20% of European banks offer crypto services today. He points to Switzerland as a blueprint. 

After DLT legislation passed, roughly three quarters of leading Swiss banks added digital asset services. He expects Europe to follow the same trajectory under MiCA.

The UK is adding pressure. The FCA BANK's proposed crypto framework won't create a standalone regime. It integrates crypto firms into existing financial services regulation. Steven Lightstone of Morgan Lewis: "A crypto firm will be treated like any normal traditional financial institution." 

The CASS client asset requirements alone could push smaller crypto firms toward mergers or acquisitions by traditional firms that already have those controls in place.

Banks already have the distribution, the compliance infrastructure, and the client relationships. They are more likely to rely on crypto infrastructure providers for custody, brokerage, staking, and tokenization rather than building it in-house. That makes licensed crypto firms with working banking relationships and custody infrastructure the primary acquisition targets.

From what I see working with crypto and fintech companies on licensing, the firms that become acquisition targets won't be chosen for having the best product. They'll be chosen for having solved compliance, banking access, and operational infrastructure, because those took years to build and can't be replicated quickly.

What does your compliance and banking infrastructure look like if consolidation reaches your market?

posts.title: Everyone looks Revolut and sees a fintech that added crypto.
posts.author: Sam Wellalage BSC MA
posts.snippet:
Everyone looks Revolut and sees a fintech that added crypto.
 
Not really.
 
Look at the licence stack instead.
 
Revolut currently holds a full UK banking licence, granted by the PRA in March. A Lithuanian banking licence covering the EU since 2018. A MiCA licence via Cyprus that passports into 30 EEA markets. FCA cryptoasset registration. In-principle VARA approval in Dubai. And a US banking application filed in March.
 
A regulated bank and a regulated crypto exchange, inside one group, under one board.
 
This is what I mean by "the new economy".
 
And hiring for it takes a different playbook.
 
The UK licence sat in mobilisation for close to twenty months. Twelve is normal. The PRA held it there over risk management, compliance and operational resilience.
 
Not technology. Not capital.
 
People.
 
The licence cleared when they had the right people in the seats.
 
Then watch what the perimeter does to the product. Revolut is delisting USDT across the EEA and Switzerland by 31 August, because Tether did not seek MiCA authorisation and Revolut holds a MiCA licence.
 
The compliance perimeter now decides what you can sell.
 
Not growth. Not trading.
 
That is what a crypto business looks like when it runs inside a bank's control environment.
 
This is the convergence, and Revolut is the cleanest single example of it.
 
TradFi is building crypto. Crypto firms are becoming banks. And a third group is arriving at the same place from the fintech side, collecting banking and crypto permissions in parallel.
 
All three are hiring the same scarce person.
 
Someone who can satisfy a prudential regulator and understand on-chain risk. Someone who has carried both, in a real seat, through a real examination.
 
That is the different playbook. You stop screening for the side someone came from, and start screening for whether they have held the perimeter.
 
I have been placing into this market since 2014.
 
Ten years ago you hired for one side or the other.
 
Now the whole job is finding the people who have lived on both.

posts.title: We're watching three separate crises converge into one opportunity — and most institutional investors still don't see it.
posts.author: Sergei Sergienko
posts.snippet:
We're watching three separate crises converge into one opportunity — and most institutional investors still don't see it.

China's approach to information control during COVID wasn't a public health policy. It was a stress test of centralized systems under real pressure. Meanwhile, the technical debunking happening around consensus mechanisms shows us that trust in traditional intermediaries is failing faster than we thought. And now pension funds are finally asking the question they should have asked five years ago: what happens when your treasury is denominated in currency nobody controls?

Here's what's actually happening beneath the surface.

When governments face genuine emergencies, centralized information systems collapse first. The bottleneck isn't capability — it's trust. People stop believing the official diagnosis because the official source has incentive misalignment. In crypto terms, that's a consensus failure. The same institutions telling you institutional adoption is slow are the ones whose legitimacy crumbles the moment real stress hits.

The technical arguments about handshakes and protocol verification matter less than you think. What matters is this: the world is building parallel systems of verification because it has to. Not because crypto evangelists won in a debate. Because the existing system proved it couldn't handle the job.

Pension funds buying Bitcoin isn't about returns. It's about optionality. They're not betting on the price. They're buying insurance against the scenario where their currency printer breaks and nobody trusts the repair manual. That's not greed — that's fiduciary responsibility finally catching up to reality.

In Africa, the most practical crypto story is not about finding the next 100x token.

It is about an importer trying to complete an ordinary order.

Imagine a Nigerian buyer ordering $10,000 of small appliances from China. The price is agreed on Monday. He has enough naira, but cannot access dollars immediately.

By Friday, the exchange rate has moved again.

His cost is higher, the supplier is still waiting, and both sides begin to doubt the deal. A real order can disappear—not because the product is wrong, but because the payment route is too slow and the currency is too unstable.

This is why stablecoins have a real use case in Africa.

For some traders, USDT or USDC is not simply a crypto asset. It works more like a digital dollar: a temporary store of working capital and, sometimes, a faster way to pay an overseas supplier.

But stablecoins and small speculative tokens are not solving the same problem.

If a market already struggles with inflation and currency volatility, another token with weak liquidity and no real use only adds issuer, liquidity and fraud risk. Without a real payment, trade or consumption scenario, most “small coins” remain speculation.

The stronger opportunity is not to launch another African token. It is to build the infrastructure around real transactions.

A buyer should be able to pay local currency to a licensed provider, complete business verification, convert the funds into a stablecoin and pay a verified supplier. The supplier should receive a clear transaction record and convert the funds through a compliant channel.

The difficult part sits behind the interface: KYC, KYB, source-of-funds checks, local liquidity, exchange rates, transaction monitoring, accounting and dispute resolution.

That is where I see the real business opportunity—cross-border collection, small-value trade settlement, reconciliation and protection of working capital.

Regulation remains the dividing line. Nigeria and South Africa are moving digital-asset activity toward licensing and supervision, but rules and enforcement still differ across African markets.

Stablecoins will not solve Africa’s monetary problems. Wider adoption may even accelerate digital dollarisation and weaken demand for local currencies.

But used carefully, they can reduce friction in real trade.

The best product may be one where the African buyer and Chinese supplier barely notice the blockchain. They only notice that payment is faster, the cost is clearer and the money is safer.

That, in my view, is the real digital-currency opportunity in Africa.

posts.title: 10 Common Misconceptions About Travel Rule
posts.author: Pawan Chawla
posts.snippet:
10 Common Misconceptions About Travel Rule

Travel Rule is one of the most discussed and most misunderstood requirement in the digital assets space. Below are some of the biggest misconceptions:

1. “Travel Rule is only for cross-border payments.”

Not necessarily.

In reality, Travel Rule requirements can apply to both domestic and cross-border transfers, depending on the jurisdiction and the regulations that have been adopted.

2. “Travel Rule was created for crypto.”

It wasn’t.

The Travel Rule has existed in traditional finance for decades. Regulators later extended similar principles to virtual assets as crypto became mainstream. 

3. “The travel rule information travels on the blockchain.”

It doesn’t.

A blockchain records things like wallet addresses, transaction amounts, and timestamps.

The information required by the Travel Rule—such as details about the sender and recipient—is generally exchanged off-chain between regulated institutions.

4. “Every stablecoin payment is covered by the Travel Rule.”

No.

It depends on who is involved, not just what asset is being transferred.

A transfer between two regulated exchanges is very different from one between two self-custody wallets.

5. “The Travel Rule applies to everyone.”

It doesn’t.

The obligations generally apply to regulated financial institutions and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), not simply because someone owns a crypto wallet.


6. “A wallet address tells you who owns it.”

If only it were that simple.

A wallet address identifies an account on a blockchain. It doesn’t automatically identify the person or business behind it.

That’s why identity verification remains such an important part of compliance.


7. “The blockchain solves Travel Rule compliance.”

The blockchain solves value transfer.

The Travel Rule solves an information-sharing problem.

These are two different things.


8. “Travel Rule compliance is the same as KYC.”

They’re related, but they’re not the same.

KYC helps establish who your customer is.

Travel Rule governs what information regulated institutions need to exchange when certain transfers take place.

9. “The Travel Rule is an AML solution.”

Not by itself.

It’s one piece of a much larger compliance framework that also includes sanctions screening, transaction monitoring, fraud detection, suspicious activity reporting, etc.

10. “The Travel Rule is a solved problem.”

This is probably the biggest misconception.

The core idea hasn’t changed: when value moves, certain information should move with it.

What’s changing is how value moves.

Stablecoins, Self-custody wallets., Decentralized finance, AI agents.

Each introduces questions the original framework wasn’t designed to answer.

⸻

Travel Rule isn’t really about moving information.

It’s about preserving trust and accountability as money moves through an increasingly digital world.

#TravelRule #Stablecoins #CrossBorderPayments

On point 4, how are VASPs handling Travel Rule data-sharing in practice when one leg of a transfer is a regulated exchange and the other is an unhosted wallet — is the industry converging on a standard, or is this still a patchwork of unilateral policies?

One of the biggest mistakes in AML/KYC is applying the same level of due diligence to every customer.

A listed company, a charity, a trust, a crypto business, and a shell company may all look legitimate on paper—but their risk profiles can be dramatically different.

That's why understanding Entity Types and Their Associated Risks is fundamental to effective AML compliance.

🏢 Common Entity Types & Risk Considerations

👤 Individuals ✅ Simple ownership structure ✅ Easier identification

⚠ Risks: • Identity Theft • Mule Accounts • Fraudulent Documentation

🏭 Private Limited Companies ✅ Clear business purpose ✅ Structured governance

⚠ Risks: • Hidden Beneficial Owners • Complex Corporate Structures • Undisclosed Related Parties

🌐 Public Listed Companies ✅ High transparency ✅ Regulatory oversight

⚠ Risks: • Cross-border exposure • Complex subsidiaries • Regulatory violations

🤝 Partnerships & LLPs ⚠ Risks: • Control exercised by multiple partners • Ownership changes • Unclear source of wealth

🏛 Trusts & Foundations ⚠ Higher AML Focus Area

Risks Include: • Opaque ownership • Complex beneficiary structures • Wealth concealment mechanisms • Multi-jurisdiction arrangements

❤️ Non-Profit Organizations (NGOs/NPOs) ⚠ Risks: • Terrorist Financing Exposure • Misuse of donations • Cross-border fund movement • Weak governance controls

🚨 High-Risk Entity Types Requiring Enhanced Scrutiny

🔴 Shell Companies

Common Red Flags: ❌ No genuine business activity ❌ Nominee Directors ❌ Virtual addresses ❌ Hidden ownership structures

🔴 Money Services Businesses (MSBs)

Examples: ✅ Remittance Companies ✅ Currency Exchanges

Risks: ❌ High cash activity ❌ Rapid movement of funds ❌ Cross-border transfers

AI GOVERNANCE SERIES · POST 5 OF 7
⚠️ NIS2 PROBABLY ISN’T YOUR PROBLEM.

But you should be able to prove why.

Every framework in this series demands attention.

This one mostly requires the opposite: knowing when not to build another compliance programme.

NIS2 is the EU’s expanded cybersecurity directive. It is broad, serious and far-reaching.

But for financial-services firms, much of it is displaced by DORA.

⚖️ The reason: lex specialis

Where a general law and a more specific law overlap, the specific regime takes precedence.

For financial entities:

➡️ NIS2 is the general cybersecurity framework
➡️ DORA is the specific regime governing ICT risk, resilience and incident reporting
➡️ On overlapping matters, DORA applies and NIS2 steps back

In practical terms, if you completed the DORA analysis from the previous post, you have probably already addressed the substance that NIS2 would otherwise cover.

You do not need two regulatory engines running on the same track.

🔍 Where NIS2 can still surface
🏢 Mixed corporate groups

A group may contain non-financial entities — such as technology, digital-services or infrastructure businesses — that fall directly within NIS2 in their own right.

🤝 Third-party suppliers and counterparties

A supplier, partner or counterparty may be NIS2-regulated and push security, notification or assurance requirements into your contracts.

🇬🇧 And do not forget the home fixture

The UK is not bound by NIS2.

However:

➡️ The UK is developing its own cyber and resilience regime
➡️ The FCA’s operational-resilience requirements already apply
➡️ UK firms must continue managing ICT, outsourcing and third-party risk
➡️ Your resources should follow the rules that actually govern your business

✅ THE SOLUTION

1️⃣ Document the carve-out

Record why DORA operates as lex specialis for the financial entity and where NIS2 is displaced.

Do not let the same question be reopened at every audit.

2️⃣ Screen the wider group

Identify any non-financial group entities that may fall within NIS2 directly.

3️⃣ Review contractual flow-down

Check contracts for NIS2-driven obligations imposed by regulated suppliers, partners or counterparties.

4️⃣ Prioritise the UK regime

Direct your cyber investment towards:

➡️ FCA operational resilience
➡️ ICT and third-party risk management
➡️ Incident response and reporting
➡️ The developing UK cyber-resilience framework

The governance skill is not collecting every framework.

It is knowing which framework applies, why it applies — and where your resources should go.

Next: The sleeper issue in this series — product-liability reform, and how today’s compliance gaps could become tomorrow’s courtroom evidence.

Julie Darmudas
Western Circle Limited

#AIGovernance #FCA #Compliance #AICompliance #ConsumerDuty

comments.text: Worth flagging the group-structure carve-out point further: even where DORA displaces NIS2 for the regulated entity, incident classification thresholds differ enough between the two regimes that a group running only the DORA playbook can still miss a NIS2-triggering event at a non-financial subsidiary.

For mixed groups, who in your experience ends up owning the screening exercise — group compliance, or the local entity most exposed to NIS2? We see this ownership gap cause reporting delays more often than the substantive lex specialis analysis itself.

AI GOVERNANCE SERIES · POST 4 OF 7
🚨 DORA: THE EU RULE THAT CAN REACH UK FIRMS THROUGH THE BACK DOOR

The Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied across EU financial services since 17 January 2025.

Many UK firms have filed it under “not us”.

Often, that is correct. But DORA can still reach into a UK operation through its group structure, technology contracts or services supplied to an EU financial entity.

DORA is not an AI regulation. It governs ICT risk and operational resilience.
But AI systems are ICT assets — and AI suppliers are ICT third parties.

That means DORA can wrap around your AI estate without mentioning “AI” once.

🔙 TWO BACK DOORS

🏢 GROUP STRUCTURE

A UK entity within an EU financial group may need to support group-level DORA obligations, including consolidated registers, controls, testing and incident processes.

🔗 ICT SUPPLY CHAIN

A UK provider supplying AI, cloud, software or other ICT services to an EU financial entity should expect DORA requirements to flow into due diligence, audit rights, security obligations, incident support and termination clauses.

DORA rests on five pillars:

→ ICT risk management
→ Major incident reporting
→ Resilience testing
→ ICT third-party risk management
→ Information sharing

⚠️ TWO FEATURES BITE HARDEST

📋 THE REGISTER OF INFORMATION

EU financial entities must maintain a prescribed inventory of their contractual arrangements with ICT third-party service providers.

If your technology supports an EU client, your client will need accurate information from you.

⏱️ INCIDENT REPORTING

For a major ICT-related incident, the reporting timetable is tight:

→ Initial notification: within four hours of classification — and no later than 24 hours after detection

→ Intermediate report: within 72 hours of the initial notification

→ Final report: within one month of the intermediate report

✅ THE ACTION PLAN

1️⃣ Determine your position: EU financial entity, UK group operation, ICT supplier or genuinely outside the DORA chain.

2️⃣ Document that assessment. “We assumed it did not apply” is not a defensible control.

3️⃣ Review contracts with EU financial-sector clients before DORA clauses arrive on their timetable.

4️⃣ Add AI systems and AI suppliers to the same ICT inventory used for operational resilience and third-party risk.

5️⃣ Align incident response, escalation and supplier notification processes to DORA’s reporting clock.

🎯 THE KEY POINT

You do not need to be directly regulated under DORA for DORA to change your contracts, evidence obligations and incident response.

Sometimes regulation reaches you through the client — not the regulator.

Next: NIS2 — and why many FCA-regulated firms can largely stop worrying about it.

Western Circle Limited

NIS2 adds a layer of complexity that's directly relevant to the insurance picture. A notified NIS2 incident is also a potential cyber claim event and the data quality of how that incident was recorded and managed will matter both to the regulator and to the insurer.

The firms navigating this most effectively are the ones who've connected the incident record to the claims record so the risk story they tell underwriters is built from the same data that manages their regulatory obligations, not assembled from two separate systems.
